specStatements.text: Acids react with some metals to produce salts and hydrogen.
(HT only) Students should be able to:
explain in terms of gain or loss of electrons, that these are redox reactions
identify which species are oxidised and which are reduced in given chemical equations. Knowledge of reactions limited to those of magnesium, zinc and iron with hydrochloric and sulfuric acids.

Acids are neutralised by alkalis (eg soluble metal hydroxides) and bases (eg insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides) to produce salts and water, and by metal carbonates to produce salts, water and carbon dioxide.
The particular salt produced in any reaction between an acid and a base or alkali depends on:
the acid used (hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates, sulfuric acid produces sulfates)
the positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate.
Students should be able to:
predict products from given reactants
use the formulae of common ions to deduce the formulae of salts.

Soluble salts can be made from acids by reacting them with solid insoluble substances, such as metals, metal oxides, hydroxides or carbonates. The solid is added to the acid until no more reacts and the excess solid is filtered off to produce a solution of the salt.
Salt solutions can be crystallised to produce solid salts.
Students should be able to describe how to make pure, dry samples of named soluble salts from information provided.

Required practical 1: preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate using a Bunsen burner to heat dilute acid and a water bath or electric heater to evaporate the solution.
Acids produce hydrogen ions (H⁺ ) in aqueous solutions.
Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions (OH⁻ ).
The pH scale, from 0 to 14, is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution, and can be measured using universal indicator or a pH probe.
A solution with pH 7 is neutral. Aqueous solutions of acids have pH values of less than 7 and aqueous solutions of alkalis have pH values greater than 7.

Students should be able to:
describe the use of universal indicator or a wide range indicator to measure the approximate pH of a solution
use the pH scale to identify acidic or alkaline solutions.
The volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other can be measured by titration using a suitable indicator.
Students should be able to:
describe how to carry out titrations using strong acids and strong alkalis only (sulfuric, hydrochloric and nitric acids only) to find the reacting volumes accurately
(HT Only) calculate the chemical quantities in titrations involving concentrations in mol/dm³ and in g/dm³ .
Required practical 2: (chemistry only) determination of the reacting volumes of solutions of a strong acid and a strong alkali by titration.
(HT only) determination of the concentration of one of the solutions in mol/dm³ and g/dm³ from the reacting volumes and the known concentration of the other solution.
A strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution. Examples of strong acids are hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids.
A weak acid is only partially ionised in aqueous solution. Examples of weak acids are ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids.
For a given concentration of aqueous solutions, the stronger an acid, the lower the pH.
As the pH decreases by one unit, the hydrogen ion concentration of the solution increases by a factor of 10.
Students should be able to:
use and explain the terms dilute and concentrated (in terms of amount of substance), and weak and strong (in terms of the degree of ionisation) in relation to acids
describe neutrality and relative acidity in terms of the effect on hydrogen ion concentration and the numerical value of pH (whole numbers only).

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of reactions limited to those of magnesium, zinc and iron with hydrochloric and sulfuric acids.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every acid-metal reaction used in this section - in the concepts, the misconceptions and the questions - is one of magnesium, zinc or iron with hydrochloric or sulfuric acid. No other metal is set as a reaction to be recalled or balanced: copper appears only as a metal that does not react, which is what makes 'some metals' in the statement meaningful, and no nitric acid reaction with a metal is written anywhere, because nitric acid is outside the reactions named here. The redox analysis is likewise carried out only on those six combinations, and iron is always taken to the iron(II) salt that dilute acid actually produces.

scopeNotes.statement: describe how to carry out titrations using strong acids and strong alkalis only (sulfuric, hydrochloric and nitric acids only)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every titration in this section uses hydrochloric, nitric or sulfuric acid against a strong alkali such as sodium or potassium hydroxide. No titration is set with ethanoic acid, citric acid, carbonic acid or ammonia solution, and no question asks about the shape of a pH curve or about buffering, which would require weak acid behaviour. The strong/weak distinction is taught only where 4.4.2.6 asks for it, and is never carried into the titration method or the titration calculations.

scopeNotes.statement: Required practical 2: (chemistry only) determination of the reacting volumes of solutions of a strong acid and a strong alkali by titration.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The titration practical is presented as the separate GCSE Chemistry required practical it is. All of the titration material - apparatus, technique, concordant titres and the calculations - is confined to 4.4.2.5 and is not folded into the neutralisation or salt preparation material of 4.4.2.2 and 4.4.2.3, which every student meets. Nothing elsewhere in this section assumes a student has carried out a titration.

scopeNotes.statement: describe neutrality and relative acidity in terms of the effect on hydrogen ion concentration and the numerical value of pH (whole numbers only).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every pH value used in the strong and weak acid material is a whole number, and every comparison of hydrogen ion concentration is a whole power of ten that follows from a whole-number change in pH. No item asks a student to calculate a pH, to work with a pH such as 3.4, or to use a logarithm, and no hydrogen ion concentration is ever expressed as a number in mol/dm³. Comparisons are always stated as 'ten times' or 'one hundred times', which is what a whole-number pH difference supports.

scopeNotes.statement: using a Bunsen burner to heat dilute acid and a water bath or electric heater to evaporate the solution
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The apparatus is taught exactly as the statement assigns it: the Bunsen burner warms the dilute acid to speed up the reaction with the insoluble solid, and the salt solution is then evaporated using a water bath or electric heater, not a Bunsen flame. Questions on the practical test that assignment rather than allowing any heat source at any stage, and no item asks students to evaporate the solution to dryness over a flame.

concepts.definition: A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal. The acid supplies the negative part of the salt and the metal, base, alkali or carbonate supplies the positive metal ion, so magnesium and hydrochloric acid give the salt magnesium chloride.

concepts.term: Reaction of an acid with a metal
concepts.definition: Acids react with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen. For example magnesium and hydrochloric acid give magnesium chloride and hydrogen: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The hydrogen gas comes from the hydrogen in the acid, not from the metal.

Only some metals react with dilute acids. Magnesium, zinc and iron all react to give a salt and hydrogen, at different rates. Copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, so no salt and no hydrogen are produced when it is added to them.
Loss of electrons. When a metal reacts with an acid the metal atom loses electrons to form a positive metal ion, so the metal is oxidised. Magnesium loses two electrons: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.
Gain of electrons. When a metal reacts with an acid the hydrogen ions gain the electrons the metal has lost and become hydrogen molecules, so the hydrogen ions are reduced: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.

A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together, because electrons lost by one species are gained by another. Reactions of acids with metals are redox reactions: the metal loses electrons while the hydrogen ions gain them.

concepts.term: Half equations for acid and metal
concepts.definition: Separate equations showing the electrons lost and gained. For zinc with sulfuric acid: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. The two electrons lost by each zinc atom are the two gained by the pair of hydrogen ions.

concepts.term: Identifying the species oxidised and reduced
concepts.definition: In an equation for a metal and an acid, the metal atom is oxidised because it ends up as a positive ion, and the hydrogen ions are reduced because they end up as hydrogen molecules. In Fe + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂ the iron is oxidised and the hydrogen ions are reduced; the sulfate ion is unchanged.
A soluble base, for example a soluble metal hydroxide such as sodium hydroxide. Its aqueous solution contains hydroxide ions, and it neutralises an acid to produce a salt and water.

A substance that neutralises an acid to produce a salt and water, for example an insoluble metal hydroxide or a metal oxide such as copper(II) oxide. Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis, so every alkali is a base but not every base is an alkali.
The reaction of an acid with a base or alkali to produce a salt and water. For example: HNO₃ + KOH → KNO₃ + H₂O, and CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O.

concepts.term: Reaction of an acid with a metal carbonate
concepts.definition: Metal carbonates neutralise acids to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide. For example: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The carbon dioxide is what makes the mixture fizz, and it is the only one of the three reactions of acids here that gives a gas containing carbon.

concepts.term: The acid decides the second part of the salt name
concepts.definition: Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates and sulfuric acid produces sulfates. So any salt made using nitric acid is a nitrate, whatever metal compound it was made from.

concepts.term: The base, alkali or carbonate decides the metal part
concepts.definition: The positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate become the positive ions in the salt. Zinc oxide gives a zinc salt, potassium hydroxide gives a potassium salt and calcium carbonate gives a calcium salt, whichever acid is used.

Name the metal from the base, alkali or carbonate and the ending from the acid, then add the other products: water for a base or alkali, and water and carbon dioxide for a carbonate. Zinc carbonate with sulfuric acid therefore gives zinc sulfate, water and carbon dioxide.
The charges needed to build salt formulae, for example Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Al³⁺ for the positive ions and Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, OH⁻, SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻, O²⁻ for the negative ions.

concepts.term: Deducing the formula of a salt
concepts.definition: Combine the ions in the ratio that makes the total positive charge equal the total negative charge, then write the numbers as subscripts, using brackets round an ion made of more than one atom. Mg²⁺ with NO₃⁻ needs two nitrates, giving Mg(NO₃)₂; Al³⁺ with SO₄²⁻ needs a 2:3 ratio, giving Al₂(SO₄)₃.

concepts.term: Making a soluble salt from an insoluble solid
concepts.definition: Soluble salts can be made from acids by reacting them with solid insoluble substances such as metals, metal oxides, hydroxides or carbonates. The solid is added to the acid until no more reacts, which makes sure all the acid is used up and nothing acidic is left in the product.

Because the solid is insoluble and is added in excess, the leftover solid can be filtered off. The excess solid stays on the filter paper as the residue and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate, which is the part that is kept.

Salt solutions can be crystallised to produce solid salts. Some of the water is evaporated to leave a more concentrated solution, which is then left so that crystals form as it cools; the crystals are removed and dried, for example by patting them between filter papers.

concepts.term: Required practical 1: making a pure, dry soluble salt
concepts.definition: An insoluble oxide or carbonate is added to dilute acid that has been warmed with a Bunsen burner, until no more reacts. The excess solid is filtered off, and the salt solution is then evaporated using a water bath or electric heater and left to crystallise, giving a pure, dry sample of the salt.
Acids produce hydrogen ions (H⁺) in aqueous solutions. It is these hydrogen ions in the solution that make it acidic, so an acid only shows acidic behaviour once it is dissolved in water.

Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions (OH⁻). Sodium hydroxide solution and potassium hydroxide solution are alkaline because of these hydroxide ions, not because of the metal ion present.
A scale from 0 to 14 that measures the acidity or alkalinity of a solution. It can be measured using universal indicator or a pH probe.

A wide range indicator that is added to a solution and turns a colour that is matched against a chart to give the approximate pH. It gives a rough whole-number value rather than a precise one, because the answer depends on judging a colour.

An instrument that is dipped into a solution and displays the pH as a number. It measures the pH of a solution directly and does not depend on matching a colour, so it can give a value to a decimal place.

concepts.term: Neutral, acidic and alkaline pH values
concepts.definition: A solution with pH 7 is neutral. Aqueous solutions of acids have pH values of less than 7 and aqueous solutions of alkalis have pH values greater than 7, so pH 3 is acidic and pH 11 is alkaline.

In neutralisation reactions between an acid and an alkali, hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to produce water. The reaction is represented by H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). The salt does not appear, because its ions stay in solution unchanged.
A method in which the volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other are measured, using a suitable indicator to show when the reaction is just complete.

A pipette is used to measure a fixed volume of one solution into a conical flask and a few drops of indicator are added. The other solution is added from a burette, swirling, until the indicator changes colour permanently; the burette readings before and after give the titre.

A single-colour-change indicator such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange is used, because it changes sharply at the end point. A rough titration is done first, then repeats; titres within 0.10 cm³ of each other are concordant and only those are averaged.

concepts.term: Amount of substance in a solution
concepts.definition: The number of moles in a measured volume of solution is found from moles = concentration in mol/dm³ × volume in dm³. A volume measured in cm³ must be divided by 1000 first, so 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ solution contains 0.00250 mol.

concepts.term: Finding a concentration from a titration
concepts.definition: The moles of the known solution are calculated, the balanced equation gives the moles of the unknown, and that is divided by the unknown's volume in dm³ to give its concentration in mol/dm³. Multiplying by the relative formula mass converts mol/dm³ into g/dm³.
An acid that is completely ionised in aqueous solution, so every acid molecule releases its hydrogen ion. Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids are strong acids.

An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution, so only a small proportion of the acid molecules release their hydrogen ions at any moment. Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are weak acids.

For a given concentration of aqueous solutions, the stronger an acid, the lower the pH. A strong acid ionises completely so it gives a higher hydrogen ion concentration, and therefore a lower pH, than a weak acid of the same concentration.
As the pH decreases by one unit, the hydrogen ion concentration of the solution increases by a factor of 10. So a drop of two pH units means the hydrogen ion concentration is 100 times greater.

These describe the amount of acid dissolved in a given volume of solution: a concentrated solution contains a large amount of acid per unit volume and a dilute one contains a small amount. They say nothing about ionisation, so an acid can be concentrated and weak, or dilute and strong.

A neutral solution has pH 7. Adding acid raises the hydrogen ion concentration and lowers the pH, and the lower the whole-number pH, the more acidic the solution and the greater its hydrogen ion concentration.

misconceptions.question: Copper is added to dilute sulfuric acid. Does a salt and hydrogen form?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only some metals react with dilute acids. Magnesium, zinc and iron do; copper does not, so nothing happens.
misconceptions.misconception: All metals react with acids, so every metal will fizz and give hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is usually first met as 'acid + metal → salt + hydrogen', which reads like a rule for all metals, and the metals used in class are chosen because they react.
misconceptions.correction: The statement says acids react with some metals. A metal only gives hydrogen if it is reactive enough; copper, silver and gold are not.

misconceptions.question: What are the products when zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Zinc chloride and hydrogen: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.
misconceptions.misconception: A metal and an acid give a salt and water, like every other acid reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutralisation by bases, alkalis and carbonates all give water, so students generalise 'salt and water' to every acid reaction they meet.
misconceptions.correction: An acid with a metal gives a salt and hydrogen. Water is produced with a base or alkali, and water with carbon dioxide with a carbonate.

misconceptions.question: Where does the hydrogen gas come from when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: From the acid. The hydrogen ions in the acid become hydrogen molecules; the magnesium becomes magnesium ions in the salt.
misconceptions.misconception: The hydrogen gas is given off by the metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The gas appears as bubbles on the surface of the metal, so it looks as though the metal is producing it.
misconceptions.correction: Only the acid contains hydrogen. Bubbles form on the metal because that is where hydrogen ions meet the electrons the metal has lost.

misconceptions.question: Copper sulfate exists, so does copper react with dilute sulfuric acid?
misconceptions.correct: No. Copper sulfate has to be made from copper(II) oxide or copper carbonate and sulfuric acid, not from copper metal and the acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper must react with sulfuric acid, otherwise copper sulfate could not exist.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper sulfate is the salt most often seen in the lab, and students assume every salt is made by the metal itself reacting with the acid.
misconceptions.correction: A salt of an unreactive metal is made from its oxide, hydroxide or carbonate. The existence of the salt says nothing about whether the metal reacts.

misconceptions.question: There is no oxygen in Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Can it be a redox reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons, and electrons are transferred here from magnesium to hydrogen ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Redox means oxygen is added or removed, so a reaction with no oxygen cannot be redox.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxidation is usually introduced as gain of oxygen, and that definition is kept even after the electron definition is taught.
misconceptions.correction: At Higher tier, oxidation and reduction are defined by electrons. Magnesium loses electrons and hydrogen ions gain them, so this is redox even with no oxygen present.

misconceptions.question: Magnesium becomes Mg²⁺. Has it gained or lost electrons?
misconceptions.correct: It has lost two electrons, so it is oxidised: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnesium gains something to become positive, so it must gain electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Gaining a positive charge' is read as 'gaining something', and the negative sign on the electron is not connected to the sign of the ion.
misconceptions.correction: Electrons are negative. Removing two negative electrons from a neutral atom leaves a 2+ ion, so becoming positive always means losing electrons.

misconceptions.question: In Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂, which species is reduced?
misconceptions.correct: The hydrogen ions. They gain electrons to form hydrogen molecules: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen ions are oxidised, because they end up as a bigger particle, the H₂ molecule.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link oxidation to becoming 'more' of something, and joining two ions into a molecule looks like a gain.
misconceptions.correction: Judge by electrons only. Each H⁺ gains one electron to become a neutral hydrogen atom in H₂, so the hydrogen ions are reduced.

misconceptions.question: What salt does iron form with dilute hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂.
misconceptions.misconception: Iron always forms Fe³⁺, so the salt must be FeCl₃.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Iron(III) compounds such as iron(III) oxide are met often, and students take 3+ to be iron's only charge.
misconceptions.correction: With dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, iron forms the 2+ ion, giving FeCl₂ or FeSO₄. Only iron(II) salts are needed for the metal-acid reactions named here.

misconceptions.question: Is every base an alkali?
misconceptions.correct: No. A base neutralises an acid to give a salt and water; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Copper(II) oxide is a base but not an alkali.
misconceptions.misconception: Base and alkali are two words for exactly the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are often used interchangeably in everyday teaching, and the first bases students meet are sodium and potassium hydroxide, which are both.
misconceptions.correction: The statement separates them: alkalis are soluble, for example soluble metal hydroxides, while bases include insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides.

misconceptions.question: What is produced when calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
misconceptions.misconception: A carbonate is just another base, so the products are only a salt and water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbonates are grouped with bases as substances that neutralise acids, so the extra product is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Metal carbonates give three products: a salt, water and carbon dioxide. The fizzing seen is the carbon dioxide escaping.

misconceptions.question: A carbonate fizzes with acid. Which gas is it?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide, because the carbonate ion contains carbon and oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Fizzing with acid always means hydrogen is being given off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first fizzing reaction met is a metal with acid, which does give hydrogen, so bubbles become linked to hydrogen.
misconceptions.correction: The gas depends on the other reactant. Metals give hydrogen; metal carbonates give carbon dioxide. Bases and alkalis give no gas at all.

misconceptions.question: Copper(II) oxide is a metal oxide. Is it an alkali?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a base, because it neutralises acids to give a salt and water, but it is insoluble so it is not an alkali.
misconceptions.misconception: All metal oxides dissolve in water to make alkaline solutions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium oxide and calcium oxide do form alkaline solutions, and these examples get generalised to every metal oxide.
misconceptions.correction: Most metal oxides are insoluble. They still neutralise acids as bases, which is exactly why they are used to make salts in the lab.

misconceptions.question: Which salt is made from nitric acid and copper(II) oxide?
misconceptions.correct: Copper nitrate. Nitric acid produces nitrates.
misconceptions.misconception: You shorten the acid's name, so nitric acid gives a nitride and sulfuric acid gives a sulfide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nitride, nitrite and nitrate all look similar, and students pattern-match on the first few letters rather than learning the three named pairs.
misconceptions.correction: The statement names the pairs exactly: hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates, sulfuric acid produces sulfates.

misconceptions.question: Zinc oxide is added to hydrochloric acid. Is the salt zinc sulfate?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is zinc chloride. Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides.
misconceptions.misconception: Salts are usually sulfates, so sulfate is a safe answer whichever acid is used.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper sulfate dominates lab work, so 'sulfate' becomes the default salt name regardless of the acid given.
misconceptions.correction: Read the acid first. The acid alone fixes the second half of the salt name, so hydrochloric acid can only give a chloride.

misconceptions.question: Nitric acid is neutralised by magnesium oxide. Where does the magnesium in the salt come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the magnesium oxide. The positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate become the positive ions in the salt.
misconceptions.misconception: The acid supplies both parts of the salt, because the acid is the reactive one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acids are presented as the substances that 'do' the reacting, so students credit them with everything in the product.
misconceptions.correction: The acid supplies the negative part only. The metal ion always comes from the base, alkali or carbonate, which is why the same acid gives different salts with different metal compounds.

misconceptions.question: Does the oxygen from magnesium oxide end up in the salt magnesium nitrate?
misconceptions.correct: No. The oxide ion takes the hydrogen ions from the acid to form water, so the oxygen leaves in the water.
misconceptions.misconception: Everything in the metal oxide must appear in the salt, giving a formula like MgO(NO₃)₂.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students track atoms into the product they are asked to name and forget that water is also a product carrying the oxygen away.
misconceptions.correction: Only the positive metal ion goes into the salt. The oxide or hydroxide combines with the acid's hydrogen to make water.

misconceptions.question: Does neutralising sulfuric acid with sodium hydroxide produce carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. An acid with an alkali gives only a salt and water: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.
misconceptions.misconception: Neutralisation always fizzes and gives off carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The carbonate reaction is memorable because it fizzes, so its extra product is attached to neutralisation in general.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon dioxide only comes from a carbonate. Bases and alkalis give a salt and water with no gas.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of magnesium nitrate?
misconceptions.correct: Mg(NO₃)₂. One Mg²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ ions so the charges cancel.
misconceptions.misconception: You just write the two ions next to each other, so it is MgNO₃.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium chloride, NaCl, is the model students copy, and there the 1:1 ratio happens to work, so charges are never checked.
misconceptions.correction: Balance the charges first. Total positive charge must equal total negative charge, which fixes the ratio before any formula is written.

misconceptions.question: Why are brackets needed in Mg(NO₃)₂?
misconceptions.correct: The bracket shows that the whole nitrate ion is taken twice, giving two nitrogen atoms and six oxygen atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Brackets are optional tidying, so MgN₂O₆ means the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The subscript is treated as a count of atoms rather than a count of ions, so the ion is broken up and its atoms multiplied out.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the ion whole and bracket it. MgN₂O₆ does not show the two separate NO₃⁻ ions and is not an accepted formula for the salt.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?
misconceptions.correct: Al₂(SO₄)₃. Two Al³⁺ ions give 6+, three SO₄²⁻ ions give 6−.
misconceptions.misconception: The charges cross over, so the 3 goes on the aluminium and the 2 on the sulfate, giving Al₃(SO₄)₂.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'swap and drop' trick is learnt as a rule without understanding, so the numbers get attached to the wrong ion.
misconceptions.correction: Check the charges in the finished formula. Al₃(SO₄)₂ gives 9+ against 4−, which cannot be right; Al₂(SO₄)₃ balances at 6+ and 6−.

misconceptions.question: How much copper(II) oxide should be added to the sulfuric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Keep adding it until no more reacts and some solid is left undissolved, which shows all the acid has been used up.
misconceptions.misconception: Add only enough oxide for it all to dissolve, so nothing is wasted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Leftover solid looks like a mistake, and students want a clear solution as the sign of a finished reaction.
misconceptions.correction: The excess solid is the point of the method: it guarantees no acid remains. It is then filtered off, so nothing is wasted.

misconceptions.question: Should the acid be in excess when making a soluble salt this way?
misconceptions.correct: No. The insoluble solid is in excess, because acid left in the mixture cannot be filtered out and would contaminate the salt.
misconceptions.misconception: Excess acid is safer because it makes sure all the solid reacts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Excess' is remembered as a general way of forcing a reaction to completion, without asking which reactant can later be removed.
misconceptions.correction: Only the insoluble reactant can be removed by filtering. So the solid, never the acid, is the one added in excess.

misconceptions.question: After filtering, which part contains the salt?
misconceptions.correct: The filtrate, the solution that passes through the paper. The salt is dissolved in it.
misconceptions.misconception: The salt is the solid collected on the filter paper.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Filtering is first met as a way of collecting a solid product, so the solid on the paper is assumed to be what you want.
misconceptions.correction: The salt is soluble, so it stays in solution and passes through. The residue on the paper is the unreacted excess solid, which is thrown away.

misconceptions.question: How should the salt solution be turned into solid crystals?
misconceptions.correct: Evaporate some of the water gently to concentrate the solution, then leave it so that crystals form slowly as it cools.
misconceptions.misconception: Boil the solution dry as quickly as possible to get the solid out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Evaporation and crystallisation are both about removing water, so the fastest way of removing it seems best.
misconceptions.correction: Strong heating can make the crystals spit out of the dish or decompose, and it gives a powder rather than pure crystals. Some solution must be left for crystals to grow in.

misconceptions.question: When the water evaporates, does the salt evaporate with it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the water turns to vapour; the salt is left behind, which is why crystals form.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating the solution drives everything off, so the salt goes as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the liquid level fall and treat the whole solution as disappearing, without separating solvent from solute.
misconceptions.correction: The salt is a solid ionic compound with a very high melting point. It stays in the dish while the water evaporates.

misconceptions.question: Can excess sodium hydroxide solution be filtered off when making sodium chloride?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sodium hydroxide is soluble, so any excess stays in the solution and would contaminate the salt.
misconceptions.misconception: Excess alkali can be filtered off in the same way as excess solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The filtering step is learnt as a fixed part of 'making a salt' and is applied to any leftover reactant.
misconceptions.correction: Filtering only removes insoluble substances. That is why the method uses insoluble metals, oxides, hydroxides or carbonates.

misconceptions.question: In Required practical 1, what is the Bunsen burner used for?
misconceptions.correct: To warm the dilute acid so the insoluble oxide or carbonate reacts faster. The solution is later evaporated with a water bath or electric heater.
misconceptions.misconception: The water bath warms the acid and the Bunsen burner is used to evaporate the solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both stages involve heating, so the two heat sources are remembered as interchangeable rather than assigned to particular steps.
misconceptions.correction: The apparatus is set by the practical: Bunsen for the acid, water bath or electric heater for the evaporation, where gentler heat protects the crystals.

misconceptions.question: Pure hydrogen chloride gas is dissolved in water. What does the acid produce?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen ions, H⁺, in the aqueous solution. Acids produce hydrogen ions in aqueous solutions.
misconceptions.misconception: An acid produces hydrogen gas, H₂, as soon as it dissolves in water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hydrogen appears as a product when acids react with metals, so 'acid' and 'hydrogen gas' become linked even without a metal.
misconceptions.correction: Dissolving produces hydrogen ions, which are what make the solution acidic. Hydrogen gas is only formed when those ions gain electrons from a metal.

misconceptions.question: Sodium hydroxide solution contains OH⁻ ions. Does that make it a source of hydrogen ions?
misconceptions.correct: No. The hydroxide ion is a single ion with a 1− charge. Alkaline solutions contain hydroxide ions, not hydrogen ions.
misconceptions.misconception: OH⁻ contains an H, so alkalis release hydrogen ions as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae are read atom by atom, so the H inside the hydroxide ion is treated as a separate particle that can break away.
misconceptions.correction: OH⁻ stays together as one ion in solution. It is the ion that reacts with H⁺ from an acid to make water.

misconceptions.question: What is the range of the pH scale?
misconceptions.correct: From 0 to 14.
misconceptions.misconception: The scale starts at 1, because you cannot have a pH of nothing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Indicator charts in books often start at 1, and 0 is read as meaning 'no acidity' rather than as a very acidic value.
misconceptions.correction: The scale runs from 0 to 14. A pH of 0 is the strongly acidic end of the scale, not an absence of acidity.

misconceptions.question: Universal indicator turns orange in a solution. What is the pH?
misconceptions.correct: About 4 or 5. Universal indicator gives an approximate pH only.
misconceptions.misconception: The colour chart gives the exact pH, so the reading is precisely 4.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The chart shows a single number beside each colour, which looks like a definite answer rather than a band.
misconceptions.correction: Matching a colour by eye gives a rough whole-number value. A pH probe is needed for a precise numerical measurement.

misconceptions.question: Is a solution that turns universal indicator orange close to neutral?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is acidic. Green is the neutral colour; orange sits on the acidic side of the chart.
misconceptions.misconception: Colours in the middle of the rainbow, like orange or yellow, must mean roughly neutral.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the colours as a spectrum and treat red and purple as the only meaningful extremes.
misconceptions.correction: The colour must be matched to the chart, not judged by how extreme it looks. Red, orange and yellow are all acidic.

misconceptions.question: What does a pH probe give you that universal indicator does not?
misconceptions.correct: A numerical pH reading, which can be given to a decimal place rather than judged from a colour.
misconceptions.misconception: A pH probe also works by colour, so it is no more precise than the indicator.
misconceptions.whyItArises: pH paper, indicator and probe are all met together as 'ways of finding pH', so their outputs are not distinguished.
misconceptions.correction: The probe measures the solution directly and displays a number, so it is used whenever a precise pH is needed.

misconceptions.question: Solution A has pH 2 and solution B has pH 12. Which is more acidic?
misconceptions.correct: Solution A. Aqueous solutions of acids have pH values of less than 7.
misconceptions.misconception: A bigger pH number means more acid, because bigger numbers mean more of something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most scales in science run upwards with the quantity measured, so an inverted scale is counter-intuitive.
misconceptions.correction: The pH scale runs the other way: the lower the pH, the more acidic. pH 12 is alkaline.

misconceptions.question: Is pure water at pH 7 a very weak acid?
misconceptions.correct: No. A solution with pH 7 is neutral: it is neither acidic nor alkaline.
misconceptions.misconception: pH 7 is the weakest acid on the scale, since acids run from 0 up to 7.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The acidic region is drawn as 0 to 7 inclusive, so 7 gets counted as the last acid rather than the neutral point.
misconceptions.correction: Acids have pH values of less than 7. Exactly 7 is neutral, and above 7 is alkaline.

misconceptions.question: A solution has pH 9. Is it acidic?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is alkaline, because its pH is greater than 7.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that is not exactly pH 7 is an acid, because acids are what change the pH.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acids are met first and far more often, so 'not neutral' is read as 'acidic'.
misconceptions.correction: Use the scale in both directions: less than 7 is acidic, more than 7 is alkaline.

misconceptions.question: Should the salt appear in the ionic equation for neutralisation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The equation is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l); the salt's ions are unchanged in solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Neutralisation makes a salt and water, so the salt must be written into the ionic equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word equation for neutralisation always shows a salt, so it is expected in the ionic equation too.
misconceptions.correction: The ionic equation shows only the particles that change. The metal and negative ions stay in solution and are left out.

misconceptions.question: Is H₂O(l) → H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) the equation for neutralisation?
misconceptions.correct: No. That is the reverse. Neutralisation is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
misconceptions.misconception: The equation contains the right particles, so the direction of the arrow does not matter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students recognise the three species and match the equation on sight without reading which side they are on.
misconceptions.correction: In neutralisation the ions are reactants and water is the product, so the ions must be on the left of the arrow.

misconceptions.question: Which piece of apparatus measures the fixed volume placed in the conical flask?
misconceptions.correct: A pipette, used with a safety filler. The burette delivers the solution that is added to the flask.
misconceptions.misconception: The burette measures out the solution that goes into the conical flask.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The burette is the tall, obviously scaled piece of apparatus, so it is assumed to do all the measuring.
misconceptions.correction: The pipette delivers one accurately known fixed volume into the flask. The burette measures the variable volume added during the titration.

misconceptions.question: Could a measuring cylinder be used instead of a pipette and burette?
misconceptions.correct: No. A measuring cylinder is not accurate enough to find reacting volumes accurately.
misconceptions.misconception: A measuring cylinder measures volume, so it will do the same job.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All three pieces of apparatus measure volume, and the difference in precision is not obvious from looking at them.
misconceptions.correction: Pipettes and burettes are made to a much finer tolerance; a burette can be read to the nearest 0.05 cm³.

misconceptions.question: Why is universal indicator not used in a titration?
misconceptions.correct: It changes gradually through a range of colours, so there is no sharp end point to judge.
misconceptions.misconception: Universal indicator is the best indicator because it works over the whole pH range.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Universal indicator is the indicator students use most, and covering the whole scale sounds like an advantage.
misconceptions.correction: A titration needs one clear change at the end point, so a single-change indicator such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange is used.

misconceptions.question: Titres are 25.60, 24.20, 24.15 and 24.25 cm³. Which are used for the mean?
misconceptions.correct: The concordant ones: 24.20, 24.15 and 24.25 cm³, which lie within 0.10 cm³ of each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Average all the readings, because averaging more results is always better.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Repeat-and-average is taught as a general rule for reducing error, without the idea of rejecting a rough trial run.
misconceptions.correction: The first titration is a rough one used to find the approximate end point. Only concordant titres are averaged.

misconceptions.question: Is it enough to do the titration twice?
misconceptions.correct: No. A rough titration is done first, then repeats are carried out until concordant titres are obtained.
misconceptions.misconception: Two readings are enough, since you only need something to average.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Repeat your experiment' is often satisfied by doing it twice, and the concordancy condition is treated as optional.
misconceptions.correction: Repeats continue until at least two, usually three, titres agree within 0.10 cm³. Agreement, not the number of runs, is the test.

misconceptions.question: How many moles are in 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide?
misconceptions.correct: 0.00250 mol. The volume is converted to dm³ first: 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³, then 0.0250 × 0.100.
misconceptions.misconception: Multiply the concentration by 25.0 directly, giving 2.50 mol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The numbers on the apparatus are in cm³ and are substituted straight into moles = concentration × volume without checking units.
misconceptions.correction: The concentration is per dm³, so the volume must be in dm³. Divide the cm³ value by 1000 before multiplying.

misconceptions.question: How many dm³ is 25.0 cm³?
misconceptions.correct: 0.0250 dm³. There are 1000 cm³ in 1 dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide by 100, because centi means a hundredth.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'centi' prefix is remembered from centimetres, and the cube on the unit is not taken into account.
misconceptions.correction: A dm³ is a cube of side 10 cm, so it holds 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³. Always divide cm³ by 1000.

misconceptions.question: 20.0 cm³ of acid neutralises 25.0 cm³ of alkali in a 1:1 reaction. How is the alkali's concentration found?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the moles of alkali by the alkali's own volume in dm³, 0.0250 dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide by the acid's volume, since that is the number the titration produced.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The titre feels like the answer of the experiment, so it gets used at every stage of the calculation.
misconceptions.correction: Each concentration belongs to its own solution. Use the moles of that solution and the volume of that solution.

misconceptions.question: Does one mole of hydrochloric acid react with one mole of sodium hydroxide?
misconceptions.correct: Yes: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O is a 1:1 reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Every acid supplies two hydrogen ions, so the ratio is always 2:1.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, is often the first titration acid met, and its 1:2 ratio with an alkali is generalised to all acids.
misconceptions.correction: Take the ratio from the balanced equation each time. Hydrochloric and nitric acids give one H⁺ per molecule; sulfuric acid gives two.

misconceptions.question: A solution is 0.0800 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide, Mr = 40. What is this in g/dm³?
misconceptions.correct: 3.20 g/dm³, found by multiplying 0.0800 by 40.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide by the relative formula mass, because moles are found by dividing mass by Mr.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The mass-to-moles direction is learnt first, and the same operation is repeated when the conversion runs the other way.
misconceptions.correction: Going from moles to grams multiplies by Mr. Check the size of the answer: grams per dm³ should be far larger than a small number of moles per dm³.

misconceptions.question: How do you decide whether to multiply or divide by the relative formula mass?
misconceptions.correct: Decide from the direction of the conversion, not the size of the numbers: mol/dm³ to g/dm³ multiplies by Mr.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide the bigger number by the smaller one so the answer looks sensible.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Under time pressure students reach for whichever operation gives a tidy-looking result rather than tracking the units.
misconceptions.correction: Write the units at each step. mol/dm³ × g/mol gives g/dm³, which shows that multiplying is correct.

misconceptions.question: Is a concentrated ethanoic acid solution a strong acid?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ethanoic acid is weak whatever its concentration, because it is only partially ionised.
misconceptions.misconception: Strong and concentrated mean the same thing, so a concentrated acid is a strong acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language 'strong' describes anything intense, so it is applied to how much acid there is.
misconceptions.correction: Strong and weak describe the degree of ionisation. Dilute and concentrated describe the amount of substance in a given volume. The two ideas are independent.

misconceptions.question: What does 'partially ionised' mean for a weak acid?
misconceptions.correct: Only a small proportion of its molecules release hydrogen ions in solution; the rest stay as whole molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Only part of the acid has dissolved, so some is left undissolved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Partially' is read as partly dissolved, because dissolving is the more familiar process.
misconceptions.correction: The acid dissolves fully. It is the splitting into ions, not the dissolving, that is incomplete.

misconceptions.question: Which is completely ionised in aqueous solution, a strong acid or a weak acid?
misconceptions.correct: A strong acid. A weak acid is only partially ionised.
misconceptions.misconception: Weak acids ionise completely because their bonds are weak and break easily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Weak' is taken to describe the bonds within the molecule rather than the extent of ionisation of the acid.
misconceptions.correction: The terms describe the acid's behaviour in solution. Strong means completely ionised, weak means partially ionised.

misconceptions.question: A dilute hydrochloric acid is used in class. Is it a weak acid?
misconceptions.correct: No. Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid at any concentration, because it is completely ionised.
misconceptions.misconception: Dilute acids are weak acids and concentrated acids are strong acids.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dilute acids are the safe ones used in school, and 'weak' is attached to anything that seems less hazardous.
misconceptions.correction: Diluting an acid changes its concentration and raises its pH, but it does not change how completely the acid ionises.

misconceptions.question: Equal concentrations of hydrochloric and ethanoic acid are compared. Which has the lower pH?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrochloric acid, because it is completely ionised and so has the greater hydrogen ion concentration.
misconceptions.misconception: The stronger acid has the higher pH, since stronger should mean a bigger number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The inverted pH scale is not connected to the strong/weak idea, so 'stronger' is matched with 'higher'.
misconceptions.correction: For a given concentration of aqueous solutions, the stronger an acid, the lower the pH.

misconceptions.question: Two acids have the same concentration. Must they have the same pH?
misconceptions.correct: No. The strong acid ionises completely and so has the lower pH; the weak acid has a higher pH.
misconceptions.misconception: Same concentration must mean the same pH, because pH just measures how much acid is present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: pH is treated as a direct read-out of concentration, with ionisation left out of the picture.
misconceptions.correction: pH depends on the hydrogen ion concentration, which depends on both the concentration of the acid and how far it ionises.

misconceptions.question: The pH of a solution falls from 5 to 4. What happens to the hydrogen ion concentration?
misconceptions.correct: It increases by a factor of 10.
misconceptions.misconception: A change of one pH unit means the hydrogen ion concentration doubles, or goes up by one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The pH scale looks like an ordinary linear scale, so a step of one is read as a step of one in the quantity measured.
misconceptions.correction: As the pH decreases by one unit, the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.

misconceptions.question: The pH falls from 6 to 4. By what factor does the hydrogen ion concentration rise?
misconceptions.correct: By a factor of 100, because the factor of 10 applies to each single unit of pH: 10 × 10.
misconceptions.misconception: It rises by a factor of 10, because the factor of 10 covers the whole change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is memorised as 'a change of pH means times ten' without noticing that it is stated per unit.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply by 10 once for every unit the pH falls. Two units give 10 × 10 = 100 times.

misconceptions.question: Which contains more hydrogen ions per dm³, a solution of pH 2 or one of pH 5?
misconceptions.correct: The pH 2 solution, by a factor of 1000.
misconceptions.misconception: A lower pH means fewer hydrogen ions, because the number itself is smaller.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The size of the pH number is read directly as the amount of acid, so a small pH suggests a small amount.
misconceptions.correction: The scale is inverted: the lower the pH, the greater the hydrogen ion concentration and the more acidic the solution.

misconceptions.question: Does a neutral solution of pH 7 contain any hydrogen ions?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, but far fewer than an acidic solution. Its hydrogen ion concentration is not zero.
misconceptions.misconception: Neutral means there are no hydrogen ions at all, which is why it is not acidic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutralisation is described as hydrogen ions being used up, so 'neutral' is taken to mean none are left.
misconceptions.correction: Neutrality is the point on the scale where the solution is neither acidic nor alkaline. Adding acid raises the hydrogen ion concentration and lowers the pH from 7.

misconceptions.question: Sodium sulfate and potassium sulfate are both made using sulfuric acid. What makes them different?
misconceptions.correct: The alkali or base used: sodium hydroxide gives the sodium salt and potassium hydroxide gives the potassium salt.
misconceptions.misconception: The salt you get depends on the conditions, such as how hot the mixture is or how much water is present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reaction conditions matter in rates and equilibrium work, so students expect them to decide the product here too.
misconceptions.correction: The salt is fixed by the two reactants alone: the acid sets the negative part and the base, alkali or carbonate sets the metal ion.

mcqs.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to magnesium ribbon. Which products are formed?

options.text: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen
options.rationale: An acid reacts with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen. Hydrochloric acid gives a chloride, so the salt is magnesium chloride.

options.text: Magnesium chloride and water
options.rationale: The student applies 'salt and water' to every acid reaction, because that is the pattern for bases and alkalis.

options.text: Magnesium chloride, water and CO₂
options.rationale: The student attaches carbon dioxide to every acid reaction, having met the fizzing carbonate reaction first.

options.text: Magnesium chlorate and hydrogen
options.rationale: The gas is right but the salt is misnamed: hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, not chlorates.

mcqs.stem: A piece of copper is placed in dilute sulfuric acid and left for ten minutes. What is observed?

options.text: Bubbles of hydrogen form on the copper
options.rationale: The student treats 'acid + metal → salt + hydrogen' as a rule that covers every metal.

options.text: No reaction: copper is not reactive enough
options.rationale: Acids react with only some metals. Copper is not reactive enough to displace hydrogen from dilute acid, so nothing happens.

options.text: The copper dissolves to give a blue solution
options.rationale: Copper sulfate solution is familiar and blue, so the student assumes the metal itself must make it.

options.text: A gas forms and the mixture warms up
options.rationale: The student expects any acid and metal mixture to react exothermically, without checking the metal's reactivity.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Which statement about this reaction is correct?

options.text: Magnesium is reduced and hydrogen ions are oxidised
options.rationale: The student links becoming positively charged with gaining, so has oxidation and reduction the wrong way round.

options.text: It is not a redox reaction as no oxygen is involved
options.rationale: The student keeps the 'gain of oxygen' definition instead of using the electron definition required at Higher tier.

options.text: Magnesium is oxidised and hydrogen ions are reduced
options.rationale: Magnesium atoms lose electrons to form Mg²⁺, and hydrogen ions gain those electrons to form H₂, so this is a redox reaction.

options.text: Chloride ions are oxidised and magnesium is reduced
options.rationale: The student sees chlorine change place in the equation and assumes it must be the species losing electrons.

mcqs.stem: How are oxidation and reduction defined in terms of electrons?

options.text: Oxidation is gain of electrons, reduction is loss
options.rationale: The definitions are reversed, the same error that makes students say a metal gains electrons to become positive.

options.text: Oxidation is gain of oxygen, reduction is loss of it
options.rationale: The student gives the oxygen definition, which cannot be applied to a reaction containing no oxygen.

options.text: Oxidation is loss of protons, reduction is gain
options.rationale: The student remembers that a subatomic particle is transferred but names the wrong one; protons are not transferred in these reactions.

options.text: Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain
options.rationale: This is the electron definition used at Higher tier to show that acid and metal reactions are redox reactions.

mcqs.stem: Zinc reacts with sulfuric acid: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Which change shows the species that is oxidised?

options.text: Zinc atoms lose two electrons to form Zn²⁺ ions
options.rationale: Oxidation is loss of electrons, and Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ is exactly that, so the zinc is the species oxidised.

options.text: Hydrogen ions lose electrons to form hydrogen gas
options.rationale: The student sees two ions become one molecule and reads that as a gain, so calls the hydrogen oxidised.

options.text: Zinc ions gain two electrons to become zinc atoms
options.rationale: The student has the change the right way round in the equation but the electron transfer reversed.

options.text: Sulfate ions transfer electrons to the zinc atoms
options.rationale: The sulfate ion appears on both sides unchanged, but the student assumes every ion in the equation must react.

mcqs.stem: Which equation represents the reaction of iron with dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.text: 2Fe + 6HCl → 2FeCl₃ + 3H₂
options.rationale: The student assumes iron is always 3+, so writes the iron(III) chloride equation even though dilute acid gives iron(II).

options.text: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂
options.rationale: With dilute hydrochloric acid iron forms the iron(II) salt, and the equation balances with two HCl for each iron atom.

options.text: Fe + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂
options.rationale: A correct equation, but for the wrong acid; the student defaults to sulfates without reading which acid was given.

options.text: FeO + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂O
options.rationale: The student expects water as the product, so selects the equation for the oxide rather than the metal.

mcqs.stem: What is produced when dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with a metal carbonate?

options.text: A salt and water only, with no gas
options.rationale: The student treats a carbonate as an ordinary base and drops the third product.

options.text: A salt, water and hydrogen gas
options.rationale: The student links any fizzing with acid to hydrogen, the gas met first with metals.

options.text: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Metal carbonates neutralise acids to produce salts, water and carbon dioxide, which is the gas seen fizzing off.

options.text: A salt and carbon dioxide only
options.rationale: The student keeps the gas but forgets that water is also produced in this neutralisation.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about bases and alkalis is correct?

options.text: An alkali and a base are the same thing
options.rationale: The two words are used loosely in everyday teaching, so the student treats them as synonyms.

options.text: All metal oxides dissolve to form alkalis
options.rationale: The student generalises from sodium and calcium oxide to every metal oxide, most of which are insoluble.

options.text: A base is an alkali that will not react
options.rationale: The student has the relationship inverted and adds a reactivity idea that does not belong to the definition.

options.text: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water
options.rationale: Alkalis are soluble bases, for example soluble metal hydroxides; insoluble hydroxides and metal oxides are bases but not alkalis.

mcqs.stem: Nitric acid is neutralised by potassium hydroxide. Which salt is produced?

options.text: Potassium nitrate
options.rationale: Nitric acid produces nitrates, and the potassium ion comes from the potassium hydroxide.

options.text: Potassium nitride
options.rationale: The student shortens the acid's name to form the salt's name, giving a nitride instead of a nitrate.

options.text: Potassium sulfate
options.rationale: The student defaults to sulfate, the salt seen most often, without reading which acid was used.

options.text: Potassium hydride
options.rationale: The student builds the salt name from the hydroxide rather than from the acid.

mcqs.stem: Nitric acid is neutralised by magnesium oxide. Which ion in the salt comes from the magnesium oxide?

options.text: The nitrate ion, NO₃⁻
options.rationale: The student credits the base with the negative part and the acid with the metal, reversing both.

options.text: The magnesium ion, Mg²⁺
options.rationale: The positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate become the positive ions in the salt.

options.text: The hydrogen ion, H⁺
options.rationale: The student thinks a compound containing oxygen and metal can supply hydrogen ions to the salt.

options.text: The oxide ion, O²⁻
options.rationale: The student expects every atom of the oxide to appear in the salt, forgetting the oxygen leaves in the water.

mcqs.stem: Which products form when sulfuric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution?

options.text: Sodium sulfide and water only
options.rationale: The student shortens 'sulfuric' to 'sulfide' rather than using the named pairing of acid and salt.

options.text: Sodium sulfate and hydrogen
options.rationale: The student applies the acid and metal products to a reaction with an alkali.

options.text: Sodium sulfate and water
options.rationale: An alkali neutralises an acid to give a salt and water, and sulfuric acid produces sulfates.

options.text: Sodium sulfate, water and CO₂
options.rationale: The student adds carbon dioxide to every neutralisation, although there is no carbonate here.

mcqs.stem: Copper carbonate is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which set of products is correct?

options.text: Copper chloride and water, with no gas
options.rationale: The student treats the carbonate as an ordinary base and loses the carbon dioxide.

options.text: Copper chloride, water and hydrogen
options.rationale: The student assumes the fizzing must be hydrogen, as it is with a metal.

options.text: Copper chlorate, water and carbon dioxide
options.rationale: The three products are right but the salt is misnamed; hydrochloric acid produces chlorides.

options.text: Copper chloride, water and carbon dioxide
options.rationale: A metal carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide, and hydrochloric acid produces chlorides.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium ions are Mg²⁺ and nitrate ions are NO₃⁻. What is the formula of magnesium nitrate?

options.text: Mg(NO₃)₂
options.rationale: One 2+ ion needs two 1− ions for the charges to cancel, and the bracket keeps each nitrate ion whole.

options.text: MgNO₃
options.rationale: The student writes the two ions side by side without checking that the charges balance.

options.text: MgN₂O₆
options.rationale: The student multiplies out the bracket, breaking up the nitrate ion instead of keeping it intact.

options.text: Mg₂NO₃
options.rationale: The student puts the 2 on the magnesium, attaching the subscript to the wrong ion.

mcqs.stem: Aluminium ions are Al³⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?

options.text: AlSO₄
options.rationale: The student pairs the ions 1:1 without balancing 3+ against 2−.

options.text: Al₂(SO₄)₃
options.rationale: Two 3+ ions give 6+ and three 2− ions give 6−, so the charges balance in a 2:3 ratio.

options.text: Al₃(SO₄)₂
options.rationale: The student crosses the charges over the wrong way, giving 9+ against 4−.

options.text: Al(SO₄)₃
options.rationale: The student balances only the sulfate side, leaving 3+ against 6−.

mcqs.stem: Copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid. Why is it added until no more reacts?

options.text: To make sure all the solid dissolves fully
options.rationale: The student wants a clear solution as the sign of completion, so adds only enough solid to dissolve.

options.text: To keep some acid left over in the mixture
options.rationale: The student applies 'use excess' to the acid, without asking which reactant can later be removed.

options.text: To be sure all the acid has been used up
options.rationale: Leftover solid shows the acid has all reacted, so no acid can contaminate the salt; the excess solid is then filtered off.

options.text: To speed the reaction up as much as possible
options.rationale: The student confuses the purpose of the excess with the purpose of warming the acid.

mcqs.stem: After copper(II) oxide has been added to sulfuric acid until no more reacts, the mixture is filtered. Why?

options.text: To collect the solid salt on the filter paper
options.rationale: The student expects the product to be the solid on the paper, as in other filtering experiments.

options.text: To remove the water from the salt solution
options.rationale: The student confuses filtration with evaporation as ways of getting a solid.

options.text: To stop the reaction before it is complete
options.rationale: The student treats filtering as a way of halting the reaction rather than separating a mixture.

options.text: To remove the unreacted solid from the solution
options.rationale: The excess insoluble oxide stays on the filter paper as the residue, and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate.

mcqs.stem: A colourless solution of a soluble salt has been filtered. How is a solid sample of the salt obtained from it?

options.text: Crystallise it by evaporating some of the water
options.rationale: Salt solutions can be crystallised to produce solid salts: some water is evaporated and the crystals are then left to form.

options.text: Boil the solution dry over a hot Bunsen flame
options.rationale: The student treats crystallisation as removing all the water as quickly as possible.

options.text: Filter the solution to collect the solid salt
options.rationale: The student thinks the dissolved salt can be caught on filter paper.

options.text: Condense the solution using a cold water bath
options.rationale: The student borrows an idea from distillation, where cooling is used to recover a liquid.

mcqs.stem: A student is making a pure, dry sample of zinc sulfate from dilute sulfuric acid. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Excess sodium hydroxide could be filtered out too
options.rationale: The student applies the filtering step to any leftover reactant, although a soluble alkali cannot be filtered out.

options.text: Excess zinc oxide can be filtered out of the mixture
options.rationale: Zinc oxide is insoluble, so any excess is removed by filtering, leaving only the salt dissolved in water.

options.text: Zinc oxide must dissolve completely to be useful
options.rationale: The student sees leftover solid as an error rather than as proof the acid is used up.

options.text: Sulfuric acid must be left in excess in the mixture
options.rationale: The student assumes the acid drives the reaction, not realising leftover acid would contaminate the salt.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 1, how is the dilute acid heated and how is the salt solution evaporated?

options.text: Water bath to heat the acid; Bunsen burner to evaporate
options.rationale: The student remembers both heat sources but assigns each to the wrong stage.

options.text: Bunsen burner both to heat the acid and to evaporate
options.rationale: The student wants the water removed quickly, so uses the flame throughout.

options.text: Bunsen burner to heat the acid; water bath to evaporate
options.rationale: This is the apparatus set out in the practical: the flame warms the acid, and gentler heating is used for the evaporation.

options.text: Water bath both to heat the acid and to evaporate
options.rationale: The student picks the gentler option everywhere, forgetting the acid is warmed to speed the reaction up.

mcqs.stem: Why is the salt solution evaporated using a water bath rather than a hot Bunsen flame?

options.text: Strong heating would drive the salt off with the steam
options.rationale: The student thinks the salt evaporates along with the water rather than being left behind.

options.text: The solution must be boiled dry to give pure crystals
options.rationale: The student believes removing every trace of water quickly is the aim, which is not how crystals grow.

options.text: A flame would react with the acid left in the solution
options.rationale: The student assumes acid remains, although the solid was added in excess so that none is left.

options.text: Strong heating can make the crystals spit or decompose
options.rationale: Gentle heating protects the crystals, which may break down or be thrown out of the dish if heated too fiercely.

mcqs.stem: Which species do acids produce in aqueous solutions?

options.text: Hydrogen ions, H⁺
options.rationale: Acids produce hydrogen ions in aqueous solutions, and it is these ions that make the solution acidic.

options.text: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
options.rationale: The student has the acid and alkali ions the wrong way round.

options.text: Hydrogen gas, H₂
options.rationale: The student links acids with hydrogen gas, which is only produced when a metal is also present.

options.text: Hydride ions, H⁻
options.rationale: The student knows hydrogen is involved but gives it a negative charge, as a non-metal would usually have.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution and calcium hydroxide solution are both alkaline. What do the two solutions have in common?

options.text: Both solutions contain hydrogen ions
options.rationale: The student sees the H in OH⁻ and treats it as a separate hydrogen ion.

options.text: Both solutions contain hydroxide ions
options.rationale: Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions, which is what makes both solutions alkaline.

options.text: Both solutions contain oxide ions only
options.rationale: The student splits the hydroxide ion up and keeps only the oxygen part.

options.text: Both contain the same metal ion in water
options.rationale: The student looks for the shared cause in the metal, although sodium and calcium ions are different.

mcqs.stem: Universal indicator is added to a solution and turns orange. What can be concluded about the solution?

options.text: The solution is acidic, with a pH of exactly 4
options.rationale: The student reads the single number on the colour chart as an exact measurement.

options.text: The solution is neutral, as orange is mid-scale
options.rationale: The student judges the colour by how extreme it looks rather than matching it to the chart.

options.text: The solution is acidic, and its pH is about 4
options.rationale: Universal indicator gives an approximate pH from its colour, and orange sits in the acidic part of the chart.

options.text: The solution is alkaline, and its pH is about 9
options.rationale: The student recalls that the indicator changes colour but matches orange to the wrong end of the chart.

mcqs.stem: Four solutions have pH 1, pH 7, pH 9 and pH 14. Which statement is correct?

options.text: pH 9 is acidic and pH 1 is strongly alkaline
options.rationale: The student reads the scale as running upwards with acidity, as most scales do.

options.text: pH 7 is a weak acid and pH 14 a weak alkali
options.rationale: The student counts 7 as the last acidic value instead of the neutral point.

options.text: pH 1 and pH 14 both lie outside the pH scale
options.rationale: The student believes the scale starts at 1 or stops short of its ends.

options.text: pH 9 is alkaline and pH 1 is strongly acidic
options.rationale: Solutions of acids have pH values of less than 7 and solutions of alkalis have pH values greater than 7.

mcqs.stem: In the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali, which particles react together and what do they form?

options.text: Hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to give water
options.rationale: In neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to produce water.

options.text: Hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to give a salt
options.rationale: The student knows a salt is produced overall, so puts it in as the product of the ionic change.

options.text: Metal ions react with hydroxide ions to give water
options.rationale: The student picks the metal ion because it is the visible part of the alkali's formula.

options.text: Hydrogen ions react with oxide ions to give hydrogen
options.rationale: The student reduces the hydroxide ion to an oxide ion and expects hydrogen gas as the product.

mcqs.stem: Which equation represents the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?

options.text: 2H₂O(l) → 2H⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq)
options.rationale: The student recognises the three species but does not check which side of the arrow they belong on.

options.text: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
options.rationale: The hydrogen ions from the acid and the hydroxide ions from the alkali combine to form water.

options.text: Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → NaCl(s)
options.rationale: The student picks the equation that forms the salt, since a salt is made in neutralisation.

options.text: H⁺(aq) + O²⁻(aq) → OH⁻(aq)
options.rationale: The student uses an oxide ion in place of a hydroxide ion and ends up with the alkali's ion as a product.

mcqs.stem: A student needs the pH of a solution to one decimal place. Which method should be used, and why?

options.text: Universal indicator, as its colour gives a value
options.rationale: The student treats the colour chart as giving a precise reading rather than an approximate one.

options.text: A pH probe, because it changes colour more sharply
options.rationale: The student chooses the right instrument for the wrong reason, assuming it also works by colour.

options.text: A pH probe, because it displays a numerical value
options.rationale: A pH probe measures the solution directly and gives a reading as a number, so it can be quoted to a decimal place.

options.text: Universal indicator, as it covers any pH range
options.rationale: The student reads wide range as high precision, although the two are different things.

mcqs.stem: Solution X has pH 3, solution Y has pH 7 and solution Z has pH 11. Which description is correct?

options.text: X is alkaline, Y is neutral and Z is acidic
options.rationale: The student reads a higher pH number as meaning more acidic.

options.text: X and Z are both acidic, and only Y is alkaline
options.rationale: The student treats anything that is not pH 7 as acidic, because acids are met far more often.

options.text: X is acidic, Y is alkaline and Z is neutral
options.rationale: The student shifts the neutral point up the scale, taking 7 as the weakest acid.

options.text: X is acidic, Y is neutral and Z is alkaline
options.rationale: Below 7 is acidic, exactly 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline, so the pH scale identifies all three directly.

mcqs.stem: In a titration, which apparatus is used to measure the fixed volume of alkali placed in the conical flask?

options.text: A pipette used with a safety filler
options.rationale: A pipette delivers one accurately known fixed volume into the flask; the burette then delivers the variable volume of acid.

options.text: A burette with a tap at its base
options.rationale: The student assumes the tall scaled burette does all the measuring in a titration.

options.text: A measuring cylinder at eye level
options.rationale: The student treats all volume-measuring apparatus as equally accurate.

options.text: A volumetric flask and its stopper
options.rationale: The student picks apparatus used for making up a standard solution rather than for transferring a measured volume.

mcqs.stem: Why is universal indicator not suitable for finding the end point of a titration?

options.text: It does not work with strong acids and alkalis
options.rationale: The student invents a limitation, having learnt universal indicator as the all-purpose indicator.

options.text: It changes through a range of colours, not sharply
options.rationale: A titration needs one clear change at the end point, so a single-change indicator such as phenolphthalein is used instead.

options.text: It only shows whether a solution is acidic or not
options.rationale: The student underrates universal indicator, forgetting it gives an approximate pH across the scale.

options.text: It reacts with the acid and uses some of it up
options.rationale: The student assumes the few drops of indicator would change the reacting volumes measurably.

mcqs.stem: A student's titres are 25.60, 24.20, 24.15 and 24.25 cm³. Which titres should be used to find the mean?

options.text: The mean of all four titres recorded
options.rationale: The student applies 'average your repeats' without excluding the rough run.

options.text: The mean of 25.60 and 24.20 only
options.rationale: The student takes the first two readings, assuming any two results are enough to average.

options.text: The mean of 24.20, 24.15 and 24.25
options.rationale: These three are concordant, lying within 0.10 cm³ of each other; the first result was the rough titration.

options.text: The mean of 24.15 and 24.25 only
options.rationale: The student keeps only the extreme pair, discarding a concordant titre that should be included.

mcqs.stem: How many moles of sodium hydroxide are present in 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution?

options.text: 2.50 mol
options.rationale: The student multiplies the concentration by the volume in cm³ without converting to dm³.
The student divides the volume by 100 instead of 1000, so the answer is ten times too large.
The student divides rather than multiplies, dividing 0.100 by 25.0.

mcqs.stem: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?

options.text: 0.0800 mol/dm³
0.125 mol/dm³
options.rationale: The student inverts the volume ratio, multiplying 0.100 by 25.0/20.0 instead of by 20.0/25.0.

options.text: 0.160 mol/dm³
options.rationale: The student assumes a 2:1 ratio, as for sulfuric acid, and doubles the moles of alkali.

options.text: 0.0400 mol/dm³
options.rationale: The student halves the answer, assuming two sodium hydroxide molecules react with each acid molecule.

mcqs.stem: A sodium hydroxide solution has a concentration of 0.0800 mol/dm³. The relative formula mass of NaOH is 40. What is this concentration in g/dm³?

options.rationale: The student divides by the relative formula mass, repeating the mass-to-moles operation in the wrong direction.

options.text: 3.20 g/dm³
options.rationale: Converting moles to grams multiplies by the relative formula mass: 0.0800 × 40 = 3.20 g/dm³.

options.text: 500.0 g/dm³
options.rationale: The student divides the larger number by the smaller to get an answer that looks a sensible size.

options.text: 0.320 g/dm³
options.rationale: The student multiplies correctly but slips a power of ten when handling 0.0800.

mcqs.stem: What does it mean to say that hydrochloric acid is a strong acid?

options.text: It contains a large amount of acid per dm³
options.rationale: The student defines strong by amount of substance, which is what concentrated means.

options.text: It is only partly ionised in aqueous solution
options.rationale: The student has the strong and weak definitions the wrong way round.

options.text: It is completely ionised in aqueous solution
options.rationale: A strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution, so every acid particle releases its hydrogen ion.

options.text: It reacts with every metal to give off hydrogen
options.rationale: The student defines strength by how vigorously the acid reacts rather than by degree of ionisation.

mcqs.stem: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid. What does this tell you about its aqueous solution?
