options.text: Only some of the acid has dissolved in the water
options.rationale: The student reads 'partially ionised' as partially dissolved, because dissolving is the more familiar idea.

options.text: It contains very few acid particles in the water
options.rationale: The student confuses weak with dilute and describes the amount of substance instead.

options.text: It cannot react with metals or with carbonates
options.rationale: The student assumes a weak acid is chemically inert, although it does react, just less vigorously.

options.text: Only some of its molecules are ionised in water
options.rationale: A weak acid is only partially ionised in aqueous solution, so most of the acid stays as whole molecules.

mcqs.stem: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid of the same concentration are compared. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The hydrochloric acid has the lower pH of the two
options.rationale: For a given concentration, the stronger acid is fully ionised, giving a higher hydrogen ion concentration and so a lower pH.

options.text: The ethanoic acid has the lower pH of the two
options.rationale: The student links 'stronger' with a higher pH number, not connecting strength to the inverted scale.

options.text: Both acids must have exactly the same pH value
options.rationale: The student treats pH as a direct read-out of concentration and ignores ionisation.

options.text: The ethanoic acid has the greater concentration
options.rationale: The student mixes up strength with concentration, although both concentrations are stated as equal.

mcqs.stem: The pH of a solution changes from 4 to 2. How does its hydrogen ion concentration change?

options.text: It increases by a factor of 2
options.rationale: The student treats pH as a linear scale, so a change of two units means a change of two.

options.text: It increases by a factor of 100
options.rationale: Each fall of one pH unit multiplies the hydrogen ion concentration by 10, so two units give 10 × 10 = 100.

options.text: It decreases by a factor of 100
options.rationale: The student reads a smaller pH number as meaning fewer hydrogen ions.

options.text: It increases by a factor of 10
options.rationale: The student applies the factor of 10 to the whole change rather than to each pH unit.

mcqs.stem: Which description fits a concentrated solution of ethanoic acid?

options.text: A large amount of a completely ionised acid
options.rationale: The student takes concentrated to mean strong, so assumes complete ionisation.

options.text: Only a small amount of a partially ionised acid
options.rationale: The student links weak acids with dilute solutions and misreads concentrated as dilute.

options.text: A large amount of a partially ionised acid
options.rationale: Concentrated describes the amount of substance per unit volume; ethanoic acid is weak, so it is only partially ionised.

options.text: A small amount of a completely ionised acid
options.rationale: The student reverses both terms, describing a dilute solution of a strong acid instead.

mcqs.stem: Acid is added to a neutral solution of pH 7. What happens to the hydrogen ion concentration and to the pH?

options.text: The hydrogen ion concentration rises and the pH rises
options.rationale: The student expects the pH number to track the hydrogen ion concentration upwards.

options.text: The hydrogen ion concentration falls and the pH falls
options.rationale: The student thinks hydrogen ions are used up whenever acid and neutral solution mix.

options.text: Neither the concentration nor the pH changes at first
options.rationale: The student assumes a neutral solution can absorb acid before any change shows.

options.text: The hydrogen ion concentration rises and the pH falls
options.rationale: Adding acid increases the hydrogen ion concentration, and a greater hydrogen ion concentration means a lower pH.

mcqs.stem: Three solutions have pH 2, pH 7 and pH 12. How do their hydrogen ion concentrations compare?

options.text: pH 2 is the highest and pH 12 the lowest
options.rationale: The lower the pH, the greater the hydrogen ion concentration, changing by a factor of 10 for each pH unit.

options.text: pH 12 is the highest and pH 2 is the lowest
options.rationale: The student reads the size of the pH number directly as the amount of acid present.

options.text: All three have the same concentration of H⁺
options.rationale: The student treats pH as unrelated to hydrogen ion concentration.

options.text: Only the pH 2 solution contains any H⁺ ions
options.rationale: The student thinks neutral and alkaline solutions contain no hydrogen ions at all.

mcqs.stem: Sodium sulfate and potassium sulfate are both made using sulfuric acid. What decides which of the two salts is formed?

options.text: The acid used, as it supplies the metal ion too
options.rationale: The student credits the acid with both parts of the salt, although both salts here use the same acid.

options.text: The alkali used, as it supplies the metal ion
options.rationale: The positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate become the positive ions in the salt, so the alkali fixes the metal.

options.text: The temperature at which the mixture is heated
options.rationale: The student expects reaction conditions to decide the product, as they can in rate and equilibrium work.

options.text: The volume of water present when it crystallises
options.rationale: The student thinks the crystallisation step, not the reactants, determines which salt is obtained.
